item.title: [Sports Illustrated] The Shoulders on Which Titles Are Built: Tarik Skubal Is Calibrated for October
item.dc:creator: Tom Verducci

item.content:encoded:
In the last moment before fury overtakes calm, Tarik Skubal stands on the plateau of a 10-inch-tall pedestal of dirt and clay as an imposing and finely calibrated 240 pounds of human pitching machinery. Nothing superfluous. Nothing without purpose. Brutally efficient.
The calibrations that lead him to the mound for a playoff game are no different than for a midseason start. The pulses of electromagnetic waves over his body, the four shots of espresso, the hot tub, the peanut butter and jelly sandwich, the dynamic warmup, the 17 to 22 pitches in the bullpen ... all of it as detailed, immutable and unassailable as Newton’s second law of motion. Skubal is so detail-obsessed that he tracks the speed of the bar when he lifts weights.
“I’m always monitoring everything,” he says. “I’m making sure that I’m doing the right things to where my body is ready to go and my nervous system is ready to go out there and pitch. It’s very complex, but it’s also simple. Everything that I do has a plan. There is always a reason for everything. I don’t do anything just mindlessly.”
All of it is done so that when it comes time for the catcher to transmit the audio signal for one of Skubal’s five pitches, Skubal is good with whatever is the choice.
The planning, scheming and studying are over. It is time to accelerate particles with ferocious force. Skubal is the only pitcher on the planet who can throw 100 mph and get hitters to miss his changeup almost half the time, the highest whiff rate on the pitch among such flamethrowers who have thrown it at least 300 times. He owns both ends of the speed spectrum.
“I’m just going to go out there and compete and try to execute pitches, so I let the catchers call what they see,” he says. “There’s a lot more stuff going on cerebrally with catchers than with me when I’m on the mound. When I’m on the mound, it’s just, get the pitch. Whatever it is, execute the pitch. I don’t really want to be thinking about too much.
“The time in between starts? I’m thinking about stuff. The time in between innings? I’m thinking about stuff. But when I’m out there, I want my process to be pretty simple.”
“If I have seen further, it is by standing on the shoulders of giants.”
The quote is attributable to Isaac Newton in 1675, though it might be appropriated these days by Dodgers president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman. While the state of starting pitching declines—starters last postseason threw fewer innings than relievers and this regular season just 57% of innings—Friedman has assembled the most expensive rotation in postseason history, if not the most decorated. He did so by seizing from other teams six elite arms whose fastballs average between 95 and 98 mph.
Dodger Stadium, ever resplendent in its timeless mid-century vibe, is home to a style of pitching that also is a throwback. Los Angeles won the World Series last year by pulling from the catalog of Koufax and Drysdale. Dodgers starters threw 10 quality starts in the 2025 postseason, the most by a world champion since the 2010 Giants. Contrary to the prevailing bullpen-heavy approach, the Los Angeles starters won postseason games, not just managed them. They were 9–4 with a 2.68 ERA. Only the 1998 Yankees and 2007 Red Sox rotations won more games in this era of expanded postseasons. The rest of MLB postseason starters last year were 13–25.
The Los Angeles aces are back, and then some. To his Ocean’s Eleven of rotations—marquee-worthy names everywhere—Friedman on Aug. 1 added Skubal, the two-time defending American League Cy Young Award winner, in a heist of a trade with the Tigers. In a span of 32 months, through free agency and trades, Friedman acquired Shohei Ohtani, Tyler Glasnow, Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Blake Snell, Roki Sasaki and Skubal. They represent six regular-season and postseason MVP awards, four Cy Young Awards and $1.38 billion in salaries, or about what it cost to pay half the players in the majors in 2011.
In the Big Four of Skubal, Yamamoto, Snell and Ohtani, the Dodgers have acquired four of the five pitchers with the lowest ERA in baseball over the past four years (minimum 50 starts), with only the Pirates’ Paul Skenes having evaded their clutches. In their combined postseason careers, the Big Four are 18–8 with a 2.85 ERA.
As L.A. attempts to become the first team in National League history to win three straight World Series, the prevailing question of this postseason is not just, Can anybody beat the Dodgers? It is, Can anybody beat the Dodgers’ starters?
“For us it’s always been ideal to go into any October with the best starting pitching you can,” Friedman says. “If there are 150-plus starting pitchers with injuries, there are certainly not 30 number ones and an abundance of ones and twos. So, there’s scarcity there. This has been a perfect storm for us being able to access so many top-end talented arms in one moment in time.”
The Dodgers’ plan this postseason is a lather-rinse-repeat exercise of last October. They conserve innings from their starters in the regular season so they can turn them loose in the highest stakes games. When L.A. faced elimination in the World Series last year, for instance, down three games to two on the road to Toronto, manager Dave Roberts used seven pitchers over the final two games, all of whom started multiple times during the regular season. Game 7 was an embarrassment of riches. Roberts used six pitchers, including Ohtani, Glasnow, Snell and Yamamoto—$1.34 billion worth of pitchers in one game, with future Hall of Famer Clayton Kershaw warming in the bullpen. Yamamoto and Snell each threw more than 525 pitches in the postseason, the first pair of World Series–winning teammates to carry such a load since Randy Johnson and Curt Schilling for the 2001 Diamondbacks.
“The thought for me has never wavered,” Friedman says of building championship teams around starting pitching. “There is more appreciation for that now because there aren’t enough of those starters—the ones you can give the ball to and feel confident they will give you six or seven innings. It’s just important to be realistic with your personnel. In ’24, with the injuries to our starting pitching, our relievers were really good. The group was deep, and we leaned on our bullpen more. In ’25, our relievers were kind of going through it a little bit and our starters were rolling. And we leaned on that. I think it’s having an appreciation for what your strengths are going into October and doing the best you can to leverage it.”
The Dodgers are a modern dynasty. They are headed to a 13th straight full season with more than 90 wins. Twelve division titles in the past 13 years. Five of the past nine NL pennants. Three of the past six World Series titles. And yet before this season began Friedman, who took over as president of baseball ops in October 2014, called this the most talented team of them all. Privately, he yearned for one more player.
“We looked to do everything we could over the offseason to avoid being a buyer in July, short of a real impact-type talent,” he says. “And so, from our standpoint, our buy side list was Tarik Skubal. End of list.”
Detroit unwittingly cooperated. The Tigers went 6–22 in May, the second-worst May in franchise history. They played themselves into shopping Skubal, a free agent after the season, before the Aug. 3 deadline. President of baseball operations Scott Harris began exploratory talks with teams about Skubal in the week before the deadline. On July 31, Friedman says, “I went to sleep and I would have thought there was no chance that the deal would wrap the next day.”
The next morning, Harris and Friedman spoke again. Later in the afternoon, everything suddenly changed. Harris wanted final offers. He would present them to the Tigers’ ownership, and they would pick the winning bid within hours. According to one executive, the Dodgers sent signals they were in parallel discussions with the Mariners for pitcher George Kirby, a word on the street seen as a gambit to raise the pressure on Detroit. Friedman, however, denies that scenario. Skubal, he reiterates, was the only name on his shopping list. “If we were fortunate enough to wind up with him, great,” Friedman says. “If not, we weren’t out in the market looking for pitching.”
Friedman put three players in the package for Skubal, none of whom would hurt the Dodgers’ current and near-term plans: River Ryan, a soon-to-turn 28-year-old pitcher coming off Tommy John surgery; Double A outfielder Zyhir Hope, 21; and Class A pitcher Brady Smith, also 21. Harris accepted.
The package was a testament to the Dodgers’ treasure-hunting expertise, the secret sauce underneath their vast spending power. Ryan, a former 11th-round pick, was plucked from the Padres for Matt Beaty, a utility player and former 12th-round pick. Hope was another former 11th-round pick swiped from the Cubs when the Dodgers needed to move first baseman Michael Busch. Smith was the 95th player picked in the 2023 draft. The Dodgers turned straw into gold. And Skubal says he immediately felt comfortable changing teams for the first time, in this case to a franchise known for its abundant resources, including two team planes, one for players only.
“I mean, all the amenities are first class, you know?” he says. “All the recovery modalities, all the spaces they have, the way they treat the families, the family room ... I mean, they’re unreal.
“It’s awesome to be a part of something where the standard is winning a World Series. That’s the way everybody goes about their business, from ownership to president to GM to manager to players, and then you talk about support staff and the chefs in the kitchen, the flight attendants ... They all go out of their way to make sure you have everything you need to go out there and perform. I feel like everyone in this organization is rowing in the same direction and everybody wants a World Series just as bad as the players do.”
Says Friedman, “He has been awesome. He has seamlessly fit into the group. He has gone out of his way to try to forge relationships with teammates and staff. He is very convicted in his prep work, but also really curious.”
Skubal rocketed to an elite pitching level in 2023 with the help of a 3-D printer. The lefthander always had trouble mastering a changeup because his hand more easily supinates than pronates, meaning he lacked the natural forearm and wrist action that creates sink and fade by letting the baseball slip from his ring and pinkie fingers as the thumb turns down. Tigers pitching coaches Chris Fetter and Robin Lund introduced him to the concept of seam-shifted wake, the uneven airflow the raised seams create over a baseball. A pitcher without natural pronation can still deaden the baseball and create movement by harnessing these aerodynamics.
Lund, a former associate professor of kinesiology with a PhD in exercise science, had been hired that season from the University of Iowa. He had the Tigers use a 3-D printer to create a plastic mold that cradles half a baseball. The mold had a circular opening that let Lund draw a black dot with a Sharpie inside the horseshoe of the seams. “Keep the dot on top of the baseball,” he told Skubal, “and think about cutting across the face of the ball.”
When Skubal throws a baseball in that manner, the air catches the seams in a way that sinks and fades his changeup like a traditional changeup but without the pronation. Over the past four seasons, Skubal’s seam-shifted pitch ranks as the best changeup in baseball, according to Run Value among pitchers with at least 1,000 changeups. (Snell’s changeup is ranked No. 2.)
“Every once in a while, when I feel a little off, I’ll get it marked up and go right back to it,” Skubal says of the dotted training baseball. “But I haven’t done that in a while. It’s more just been about pitch execution, not pitch shape right now.”
The wonder of Skubal is that the game’s best changeup pitcher over those same four years also has the No. 3-ranked four-seam fastball among starting pitchers who have thrown at least 1,500 of that pitch. (Ohtani and Yamamoto rank Nos. 1 and 2.) With his natural supination, Skubal throws his fastball with a spin axis equivalent to the hour hand of a clock pointing to 11:15. “I throw a heater that’s not 100% efficient,” he says. “When it is 100% efficient, it’s actually a worse pitch. I need to cut it a little bit. I need to get like 94%, 92% efficiency because then I get more ride and a little bit more cut.”
Changeups and four-seamers account for 61% of his pitches. Sinkers, sliders and curveballs complete his arsenal, unless you include the adrenalin that makes him one of the most ferociously aggressive pitchers. Skubal has ranked first or second in first-pitch strike percentage two years running.
“The game is as analytic as ever,” he says. “You do want to get scouting reports and all that stuff. You can get as deep as you want, but for me it’s really about first-pitch strikes. It’s winning your 1–1 counts. It’s getting to two-strike counts as fast as possible because when you’re in those moments, you have the most leverage ever.
“When you get into two-strike counts, you should have all the confidence in the world. You’ve worked your ass off to get to this count. Now I’ve given myself room to get out of the zone a little bit. And sometimes I challenge guys in the zone, too, because when you get into count leverage, you have everything. Just execute a pitch, and the guy’s out.”
Skubal’s adrenalin-laced, pedal-to-the-floor style of pitching is well-suited for the postseason, in which he has made six career starts, all on the road and all with only two or three runs of support. Among the 219 pitchers who have made at least six starts in postseason history, Skubal ranks first in strikeouts per nine innings (12.7), second in WHIP (0.731) and third in hits per nine innings (5.2) and strikeouts per walk (9.33). His 2.04 postseason ERA is the lowest ever by a pitcher never to reach the World Series (minimum 35 innings).
“I love it,” he says of the postseason. “I feed off environments and energy and stadiums all in a positive way. The average velocity on the heater goes up. All the shapes kind of go up. The execution gets a little bit better, too.”
Come October, the calibrations that prepare him for the mound will not change. Skubal will stick to his mission-control like pre-launch routine:
• T-minus 150 minutes: Training room treatment with pulsed electromagnetic field therapy to relieve any soreness and stimulate blood flow.
• T-minus 120 minutes: Four shots of espresso. “That way,” he says, “I’m heavily caffeinated and ready to go.”
• T-minus 115 minutes: Hot tub followed by stretching and general body warmup.
• T-minus 60 minutes: Peanut butter and jelly sandwich. “Always Uncrustables,” he says. “[An] Uncrustable right to a toaster is the best thing in the world. They’re so convenient and they have them everywhere. And I know my stomach handles them well, so that’s why I eat them.”
• T-minus 40 minutes: Dynamic warmup to raise heart rate and body temperature.
• T-minus 30 minutes: Play catch.
• T-minus 20 minutes: Warm up on bullpen mound. “It always ends up being 17 to 22 pitches,” he says. “Seventeen to 22 throws is all it really takes for me.”
• T-minus eight minutes: Last bullpen pitch. Walk to dugout.
• T-minus one minute: A last reminder.
“The main thing that I remind myself in bigger moments is the game still stays the game,” he says. “The bigger the moment, the simpler the process needs to be. Just go do the things that make you great ... the first-pitch strikes, getting ahead, throwing strikes, getting into leverage, and getting these guys out early and often and putting them on their toes as much as you can. So, the bigger the game, the simpler my game gets on the mound.”
Skubal will stand on that plateau with his hands in front of his chest. The catcher will give him the radio-transmitted signal for the pitch. Skubal, who wears only the receiving device, not a transmitter, inevitably will agree. There is little mystery what is coming. Skubal threw a fastball on the first pitch of 153 of his 159 career starts through mid-August, postseason included.
With the ball in his glove, he will raise his hands in front of his face, peering over his mitt like a marksman through a sight. With a sidestep of his right leg, Skubal rocks his hands down to his belt. It is the quiet trigger to a delivery so violent and explosive that it is as if a starburst of fireworks shoots off 100 times a night. The right leg lifts so high his toes reach eye height. As he strides down the mound, he so separates the ball from his glove with straightened arms he seems to be stretching a giant rubber band to its breaking point. The glove points toward the upper deck, flashed to the hitter like a magician’s diversion. His shoulders are severely slanted, as if throwing a javelin.
Where is the baseball? It is low and behind him. It is as if he is reaching back. Reaching back all the way to Octobers past, when starting pitchers were the Hercules of the postseason, demigods who would squint against the flash-pops of the Graflex Speed Graphics in the pregame phalanx of photographers who posed them like heavyweight fighters. They were the stone and mortar of which championships were built.
“Starters,” Skubal says, “set the tone for everything going on. Yeah, I think that’s why teams win.”
Skubal and the Dodgers are reaching back to such an era. Whether four, five or six deep, they are the only team that can play such a style every postseason game they play. In the Big Four, the Dodgers could send a multiple Cy Young Award winner or a postseason MVP to the mound every night of October. Their methodology is as intentional as Skubal’s calibrations. Who will stop them?
Tom Verducci is a senior writer for Sports Illustrated who has covered Major League Baseball since 1981. He also serves as an analyst for FOX Sports and the MLB Network; is a New York Times best-selling author; and cohosts The Book of Joe podcast with Joe Maddon. A five-time Emmy Award winner across three categories (studio analyst, reporter, short form writing) and nominated in a fourth (game analyst), he is a three-time National Sportswriter of the Year winner, two-time National Magazine Award finalist, and a Penn State Distinguished Alumnus Award recipient. Verducci is a member of the National Sports Media Hall of Fame, Baseball Writers Association of America (including past New York chapter chairman) and a Baseball Hall of Fame voter since 1993. He also is the only writer to be a game analyst for World Series telecasts. He lives in New Jersey with his wife, with whom he has two children.

item.content:encoded:
Apparently, Mark Cuban and Andrew Friedman weren’t content conquering professional sports.
Now they’re coming for your neighborhood sports bar.
Tucked inside a sprawling 8,500-square-foot former pawn shop that dates back to the 1930s, L.A.’s newest reinvention on sports, luxury, and fine dining is born. Located on the corner of Melrose and Cahuenga sits Pawn Shop, a new restaurant and sports bar that features more than 60 televisions, two enormous media walls, private suites, and high-end cocktails galore.
Sign up for the California Morning Report newsletter
The biggest news, opinion and culture shaping California right now.
Thanks for signing up!
It’s led by founder and CEO Diego Torres-Palma and James Beard Award-winning chef Tony Messina. Together they’ve made the standard sports bar menu of chicken wings, nachos and mozzarella sticks look insulting by comparison.
A housemade wagyu hot dog, beef tallow fries, chicken liver mousse, caviar and charbroiled Maine oysters are just some of the menu’s highlights.
But the most interesting thing about Pawn Shop isn’t what’s on the walls or plates.
It’s who is behind it.
Billionaire entrepreneur and former Dallas Mavericks owner Mark Cuban is an investor. So is Dodgers’ president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman.
The list of names interested in either investing or being a part of the business is longer than a CVS receipt.
“We literally traded emails when Aaron announced he was coming back,” Torres-Palma said.
Donald isn’t the only Dodgers-or-Rams-adjacent star circling the new sports bar. Dodgers’ shortstop Mookie Betts met with the company and will now feature his Tequila Providencia behind the bar. Torres-Palma said Providencia’s CEO Rodd Rafieha’s tequila impressed his beverage team enough to earn a place in the well.
Kendall Jenner’s 818 Tequila also wanted in on the fun.
“We’re excited to have 818 Tequila featured at Pawn Shop LA,” said Lanay Jacobs, President of 818 Tequila. “It’s a lively destination that brings together sports, cocktails, and community in a way our audience will love.”
Torres-Palma has other meetings set up with L.A. superstar athletes as well.
That collection of names helps explain why Pawn Shop has quickly become less a sports bar and more a hangout spot for athletes and celebrities alike.
Former NBA player Chandler Parsons, now the co-host of the online show “Run It Back,” makes a point to stop by at least once a week.
“Pawn Shop is exactly what LA needed,” he said. “Great food, great energy, amazing people, and a genuine love for sports that you can feel when you walk in.”
Sportscaster and radio host Rich Eisen recently held his fantasy football draft there. The entire LAFC team did the same. Actor Anthony Ramos has stopped by several times. Several entertainment executives have used the space, while nearby Paramount staffers have turned its private upstairs suites into off-site work rooms.
Cuban recently visited with his son and was in awe.
“Of all the investors, Mark is probably the one that I communicate with the most,” Torres-Palma said. “He’s so pumped. Honestly, he’s probably been our top supporter.”
The timing of Pawn Shop’s opening could hardly have been better.
It arrived during the 2026 FIFA World Cup, instantly giving an unknown sports bar the kind of crowds and atmosphere most restaurants spend years trying to manufacture.
Torres-Palma compares those first weeks to hosting a wedding every few days: hundreds of customers arriving together, watching the same event and wanting food and drinks at virtually the same moment.
The peak came during Mexico’s wild Round of 16 match against England.
“I’ll never forget the roars in here,” Torres-Palma said. “That feeling is why you build these things. It’s such a crazy, loud, energetic feeling that everybody experiences at the same time.”
He even has a phrase for it: “monetizing moments.”
It sounds cold until you stand inside a room filled with hundreds of strangers collectively losing their minds over a goal. When fans of El Tri or the Three Lions look back on that historic match, they’ll remember being at Pawn Shop and sharing a memory they’ll never forget with others.
That’s what “monetizing moments” is all about. It’s also a pretty good description of the entire sports business.
The question now is whether Pawn Shop can sustain that feeling now that the World Cup is over.
Los Angeles is littered with restaurants that were once the hottest reservation in town. Sports bars and national chains have closed locations, too. Novelty disappears quickly here.
“When people say the restaurant business is brutal or very tough, I always ask them, ‘What’s an easy business so I can go do that?’” he said.
His answer to struggling competitors is considerably sharper.
“Let them quit,” Torres-Palma said. “They should have never played the game.”
That swagger only works if the product backs it up.
So far, Pawn Shop has a legitimate argument that it does.
Its biggest advantage might actually be the food. Pawn Shop feels less like somebody dressed up a sports bar as a restaurant than somebody built a serious restaurant and happened to cover it in televisions.
Customers can tell their server which game they want and staff can route it in seconds to televisions near their table. If someone wants USC football on one screen, the Dodgers on another, Texas football on a third and the U.S. Open nearby, you can get all of them and more at the snap of a finger.
During NFL Sundays, the two massive central media walls can even show different games, effectively splitting the room into competing fan bases.
“A lot of bars in L.A., we’re learning, don’t put the sound on,” Torres-Palma said. “We will fully lean in to actually having the sound on.”
It seems laughably obvious for a sports bar to play the sound of the game they’re featuring.
That’s also the point.
Pawn Shop is betting there’s a hole in Los Angeles between the neighborhood dive with eight televisions and mediocre wings and the actual stadium experience, where dinner can cost a fortune and nobody is going just for the cuisine.
“We are that clubhouse,” Torres-Palma said. “We just want to be a sports hub.”
And this is only phase one.
Pawn Shop plans original digital programming pairing athletes with Messina, including a concept in which the chef recreates a favorite childhood meal for a player. “Sinatra Tuesdays” are coming, featuring old-school Italian dinners and Hollywood-inspired programming. October will bring outdoor movie nights.
In February, the Super Bowl returns to Los Angeles, a time when Torres-Palma says companies are already approaching Pawn Shop about buyouts, pregame parties and postgame events.
After that?
Expansion.
“I think we’ll be opening up No. 2, or be close to opening,” Torres-Palma said of where he expects Pawn Shop to be by next summer. “Probably Vegas, almost certainly.”
For all the celebrity investors, tequila deals, televisions and franchise plans, Torres-Palma keeps coming back to something much simpler.
He wants people leaving Pawn Shop with a story to tell.
Whether that’s a World Cup goal, a Dodgers walk-off win in October, a Rams 4th quarter comeback, a chance encounter with an actor or athlete, or even a glimpse of a World Series trophy or Super Bowl ring.
“I just really want people to talk about Pawn Shop as a place where, like, ‘Oh, this crazy thing happened to me here,’” Torres-Palma said.
Ultimately, that might be Pawn Shop’s smartest bet.
L.A. has plenty of places to eat, grab a drink or watch a game.
But what Cuban, Friedman and Torres-Palma are betting their business on is that L.A. still needs a place where something worth remembering happens while you’re doing all three.

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers may have spoiled Josue De Paula's breakout game, but his monster home run against the Miami Marlins on Sunday sent a message: this kid may live up to his billing as LA's No. 1 prospect.
The Dodgers still have to figure out how they're going to fit him on the roster when Shohei Ohtani comes off the IL, but as long as his brief audition at the tail end of this season continues to go well, that should be a priority this offseason.
Maybe we're getting way ahead of ourselves here, but if the Dodgers figure out how to get him regular at-bats in 2027, we could be looking at the next in a long and storied line of Dodgers Rookie of the Year Award-winners.
The Dodgers have an MLB-leading 18, beginning, of course, with Jackie Robinson in 1947, the man the award is named after. Their latest winner was Cody Bellinger in 2017.
Sandwiched in between are franchise legends Jim Gilliam, Fernando Valenzuela, Eric Karros, and Hideo Nomo, just to name a few. De Paula could find himself in some very good company by the end of 2027.
Putting Josue De Paula's future Rookie of the Year campaign into context with other Dodgers greats
De Paula has been compared heavily to Yordan Alvarez, probably Andrew Friedman's greatest trade regret as the Dodgers' chief executive. Of the 12 position player Rookies of the Year the Dodgers have produced, none are quite the same archetype as Alvarez — David Ortiz, Kyle Schwarber-esque players who can flat-out hit.
But perhaps the most apt comparison is Mike Piazza, LA's winner in 1993. Piazza came into the league with far fewer expectations attached than De Paula, but both are defensively weaker position players with massive power potential and advanced plate discipline. De Paula has yet to strike out in the four games he's appeared in.
It would be unfair to expect the same kind of offensive production from De Paula that Piazza offered up in his rookie season, when he hit .318 with a .932 OPS, 35 homers, and 112 RBI to kick off what would become a Hall of Fame career.
But when the Dodgers, who are usually so enthused about their prospects, were all but champing at the bit to find him a place to play this season, that says a lot as to where they think his ceiling could be.

item.content:encoded:
gambit – noun
a chess opening in which a player risks one or more pawns or a minor piece to gain an advantage in position
Now, if your mind immediately went to the Marvel Comics character and you were confused, fair enough. Here's the clip you likely thought of, so we can all feel better and get to the heart of the essay.
And for the record, Freddie Freeman is hardly a minor piece, but giving up a major piece for tactical advantage is called a sacrifice, which wouldn't be appropriate given the circumstances here, as Freeman returned to the lineup for the September 15 game against the Cincinnati Reds.
A funny thought occurred to me while watching Freddie Freeman these last few months:
"Where did his power go? He sure seems like he's hitting into more double plays than I remember."
Looking at Freeman's stats for the year, apart from the power and RBI numbers being down a bit, nothing looks amiss. Honestly, I originally dismissed the feeling that something was wrong because Freeman was hitting up a storm for about a month after the All-Star Break.
There wasn't much power behind it, but when someone has a slash line of .367/.402/.411 over 24 games starting from the All-Star Break, pointing out fault feels like searching for a fly in the ointment. Yes, Freeman only had four doubles, eight RBIs, and nearly three times as many strikeouts as walks, but the overall body of work looked pretty good.
Freeman had a solid couple of games in Denver where he hit for doubles power and used the entire field. However, since the Denver series, where Freeman was hitting for average, he's just not.
When you aren't hitting for either average or power, alarm bells tend to finally ring.
Power drained
On September 9, Freeman was kept out of the lineup for right knee soreness and was considered day-to-day. To his credit, Dave Roberts did mention Freeman's slump on September 9.
Roberts said there was no one incident that caused Freeman's knee soreness, but he believes it has impacted his performance at the plate lately.
"Freddie does a really good job of hitting against his front side, and then when you can't do that with your front side, your right knee, then you're compromised," Roberts said. "I see there's a lot more swing-and-miss the last few days. That's just not who he is."
In the 18 games since the Colorado series until the start of play on September 15, Freeman has a slash line of .215/.338/.292. He does have his only home run of the second half, and his strikeouts-to-walk ratio is about 1.5/1 instead of 3/1 earlier in the year.
The problem is more of the eye test: Freeman is starting to finally look, and maybe move, like his age.
The splits on Baseball Savant from last year to now tell a pretty glaring tale: if you want to beat Freeman in 2026, go low and in. Also, Freeman feasted on center-cut pitches last year, not so this year.
I'm not a hitting expert, but having a diminished knee would make it harder to rotate to hit stuff middle in. On the September 13 broadcast of the finale against the Miami Marlins, Dontrelle Willis pointed out how Freeman is compromised rotationally generally, as pitches he would normally drive the other way are being weakly hit.
Even after Freeman hit a career-high and now league-high in double plays on Sunday, the Dodgers are not seriously entertaining putting Freeman on the injured list, per Katie Woo of The Athletic:
"I think it's one of those things where we've got to manage it … just pick spots to give him an off day here or there," Roberts said. "Again, we've just got to make sure he's at optimal health when we finish the season. So I think that he might not love it, but giving him a day off here or there might be beneficial."
The Dodgers don't believe an IL stint is necessary. Instead, Roberts is working in frequent off days. That's rare for Freeman, who hasn't played in fewer than 147 games in any season as a Dodger. Freeman had a scheduled day off over the Dodgers' previous nine-game homestand and also served as the designated hitter twice in that span. He wasn't in the lineup in the last game of the homestand on Wednesday, and following a team travel day, he also sat out Friday's game.
[Emphasis added.]
Freeman insists he feels fine.
Freeman hitting into two double plays and having a key miscue that contributed to the season and series loss to the Miami Marlins seems to indicate otherwise. It's worth noting that Freeman hit another tailor-made ground ball to second on a pitcher's pitch in his final at-bat that likely would have turned into another double play had Mookie Betts not doubled earlier in the frame.
"Just talking to him today, he said he felt good," Roberts said. "Obviously, the swings don't indicate that, don't validate that. On the defense, he's obviously not moving as well as he's used to.
"I think that he's doing anything and everything he can to prepare. But yeah, the last week, it's pretty obvious that he's not himself in the box."
Freeman won't be in Monday's starting lineup, Roberts said, but should play Tuesday…
[Emphasis added.]
Much like the sense one had when watching the Americanized remake of the original 1954 classic Gojira, Godzilla: King of the Monsters, one would expect a sense of deja vu right now, even with character actor Raymond Burr long dead.
Japanese Original, American Remake
I am typically not one to mince words, and I shall not do so here. Along with Dustin Nosler of Dodgers Digest, I was dead on the money regarding the Dodgers' malpractice in not acting decisively on Ohtani and his reluctance to admit injury in the face of personal dogma of success.
I argued that the Dodgers had bungled spectacularly, and events worked themselves out to prove my initial hypothesis correct on all fronts. Now the team has backed itself into a corner regarding Ohtani.
Contrary to what some might think, I did not enjoy being right. Frankly, I am correct often enough that I do not need the constant validation, unless it comes from either the Dodgers broadcast team or national media. (In which case, gimme.)
On September 11, Katie Woo of The Athletic wrote an op-ed recently that pulled few punches:
Nobody is blameless in the Shohei Ohtani injury saga. Not the Los Angeles Dodgers' front office, which should have been more proactive in protecting the team's biggest star. Not Ohtani, who downplayed the severity of his symptoms. And while hindsight is always 20-20, there were warning signs throughout the last few weeks that suggested a stint on the injured list was the safest course of action if the organization wanted to give its prized star the best possible chance at healing in time to begin the Dodgers' quest to win three straight World Series.
As the Dodgers prepare to be without Ohtani until Sept. 23 at the earliest, their biggest concern has become a reality. When Ohtani — who is expected to be placed on the injured list on Friday — does return, there is no guarantee he'll be in optimal condition for the postseason.
[Emphasis added.]
Um, excuse me? To quote one of the finest bits of media from the 2010s, I get to channel Chris Taylor for once and declare the following:
I know, Ms. Woo means nobody relevant, but words matter, and any excuse for referential comedy is a good one.
"I think that if it were a postseason game tomorrow, (Ohtani) would be in the lineup," manager Dave Roberts said Wednesday afternoon, hours before announcing Ohtani would be placed on the IL. "I think that now you're talking about two weeks, 14 days. I feel that that's substantial. He'll be in a much better place than he was today. Is it going to be to 100 percent? Probably not. But I do think that with this time that we're taking now he'll be in an adequate spot to finish the season."
Adequate is a far cry from healthy. It is fair to question how Ohtani was handled in the second half. Should he have attempted a pitching comeback, knowing his physical health was limited? Should the Dodgers have stopped that push sooner, or placed him on the injured list earlier? In their first season of managing Ohtani as a full-season two-way player, there was always going to be some trial and error. That was acknowledged from the start of the season by both Roberts and president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman. And in fairness, there was a cognizant effort to keep Ohtani as rested as possible, including a season-long six-man rotation and an attempt to maneuver Ohtani's starts to line up on games prior to a team off day, when possible.
Hindsight is generally 20/20. I am sure if the Dodgers were armed with foreknowledge in a do-over, they would not have Ohtani's best pitching starts of the year be in Houston and San Francisco … in May.
At the risk of retreading previously covered ground, we shall conclude this portion with Roberts' regret, especially considering that Ohtani tweaked his arm in his last played game and did not immediately tell anyone about it:
Looking back, it is something Roberts wish happened a week ago.
"I think if we look right now, here today, I would love to go back and put him on the IL," the manager said. "But I did feel at that moment in time, we all felt that giving him four days was sufficient. He was agreeable. Getting him out there on Monday with the hope that he would be able to play tonight. But where we're at right now, sure."
The Dodgers should have followed their own advice or learned from their handling of Ohtani to send Freeman back to Los Angeles for ten days before arriving in Cincinnati.
They didn't.
The Dodgers have calculated that whatever value Freeman can generate in the waning days of the season is greater than the potential benefit of having Freeman recuperate for ten days, having three days against the already-eliminated San Francisco Giants to use as a tune-up. Hence, the title of this essay: the Freeman Gambit.
Yesterday's game showed promise, even with a couple of moments that made one grimace. Freeman talked about how his three-hit performance likely ensured he would play on September 16.
Fabian Ardaya of The Athletic reported Roberts' comments on the health issues of players like Ohtani, Freeman, and Edgardo Henriquez after the Dodgers clinched their fourteenth consecutive postseason appearance:
"I think right now it's front of mind, it's not great," Roberts said. "But I will say this: Once you get to October, athletes have a magical way of feeling better. It happens every single year, where there's that extra adrenaline that athletes get when you get to the postseason."
The Dodgers still boast what is likely baseball's most talented roster and an established track record of postseason success that might be enough to make history. That was the heart of Roberts' toast: that the Dodgers have not yet played their best baseball.
They still can.
"We just haven't really gotten everyone all synced up at the same time," Muncy said. "So it is a scary thought to think what we could possibly do if we did that. So hopefully that's still ahead for us at the right time."
Whether the Freeman Gambit pays off over the next two weeks before the upcoming postseason tournament is an open question. Gambits are risky, even when they work.

item.content:encoded:
The other day I walked outside my apartment in New York and noticed the slightest hint of a chill in the morning air. And I could only think of one thing: the postseason is almost here. The long baseball season is drawing to a close. The delight of October awaits.
And then …
Oh, yeah. The lockout.
The next few months could reshape the future of baseball. I suppose we shall see how it goes. Until then, let’s take some questions. As always, they have been edited for clarity.
Advertisement
Which wild-card team has the best chance to upset a division winner? — bbrathizza2075
There are a lot of worthy candidates, especially in the National League. But I would have to say the Yankees, if only because on paper, the Yankees should be the best team in the American League, even if they are unlikely to catch the American League East. The Yankees lead the AL in run differential by a significant margin. No AL lineup has hit more home runs. In Cam Schlittler, they employ the Cy Young favorite. And they still have Aaron Judge.
So the Yankees would be my pick, but the talent on the other wild-card clubs is immense. The Phillies can line up Cristopher Sánchez, Zack Wheeler and, if he’s healthy, Jesús Luzardo in a five-game series. Good luck. Pete Crow-Armstrong has been the best player in baseball for a Cubs team that boasts the best offense in baseball. A healthy Nick Pivetta provides San Diego with enough rotation stability for a short series, in which their bullpen would be hellish to face. And the Padres, who would likely face the Dodgers, have shown a willingness in recent years to stand and trade blows with baseball’s reigning champs.
And, really, what qualifies as an upset? If the 98-win Rays lose to the 94-win Yankees in a five-game series, would it really be shocking? Same story with the Phillies or the Cubs facing the Brewers. These teams will be quite evenly matched. It should be an entertaining October.
Which National League fanbase would be MOST disappointed if its team doesn’t hoist the commissioner’s trophy in 2026? Big narrative-ball postseason for Brewers, Phillies and even Cubs fans in my opinion. — Jacob N.
I think it’s a toss-up between Milwaukee and Philadelphia. And I would lean toward the Phillies.
When it comes to the Brewers, a lot of folks in baseball have asked the question: If not now, when? Well, the team made clear, in part by declining to go bonkers and acquire Tarik Skubal, that it rejects the premise. And the Brewers brain trust may be wise to do so. This team is well-situated to contend in 2026, but also well beyond 2026. Jackson Chourio is 22. Jacob Misiorowski is 24. Logan Henderson is 24. Brice Turang is practically ancient at 26. Jesús Made and Luis Peña are on the way. This team isn’t going anywhere.
Right. Right?
Well …
Baltimore fans felt the same way after a 101-win campaign in 2023. Instead, they’ve watched the Orioles degrade from budding juggernaut into a last-place club. And while I do not foresee that fate for the Brewers, it remains within the realm of possibility. Misiorowski may not stay healthy beyond this season. The 2026 campaign could be this group’s best chance to win the first championship in franchise history.
Advertisement
Even so, I don’t think the psychological blow of an early exit would sting Brewers fans like it would Phillies fans. There is just so much frustration stored up within that fanbase, dating to that shocking collapse in the 2023 National League Championship Series. There are also legitimate questions about how long the window will remain open for this group. Again, it comes back to age. Kyle Schwarber is 33. Bryce Harper turns 34 in October. Zack Wheeler is 36. Trea Turner is playing below-replacement-level at 33 — and his contract will not expire until 2033. The farm system has not produced much in recent years, and Dave Dombrowski has not done well on the free-agent market.
So while Brewers fans may be infuriated about the unfairness of MLB’s system, and while they may lament another missed opportunity, they can credibly believe they will have another shot in 2027. That is harder to fathom for Phillies fans.
The first two teams to clinch playoff berths were the Rays and Brewers. Could you shed any light on the Tampa Bay model both teams adhere to? — Gary D.
Back in 2021, I wrote a lengthy feature about the Rays and their ruthless roster building. The simplest way to describe it is they make a lot of transactions, and that churning allows them to occasionally unearth stars.
Here is one example. Back in 2008, the Rays chose Tim Beckham with the first overall pick in the draft. Beckham was essentially a bust. He took five years to reach the majors and never really hit. In 2017, after nearly a decade of trying to develop him, Tampa Bay dealt Beckham to Baltimore for minor-league pitcher Tobias Myers. He spent a few seasons in Tampa Bay’s farm system before getting traded to Cleveland for a teenage prospect from the Dominican Republic. You may have heard of him by now: Junior Caminero. And Caminero has become the sort of star the Rays once envisioned Beckham could have been. The team turned a failure into a smashing success.
Now, most front offices don’t get a decade to oversee decisions like this. Andrew Friedman was in charge when Beckham was drafted. Chaim Bloom was running the show when Beckham was traded. And Erik Neander, who has worked in the organization since 2007, was the head of baseball operations for the Caminero deal. But the organizational ethos hasn’t changed all that much over the past decade.
Advertisement
Milwaukee also tends toward roster churn but is a tad less aggressive than Tampa Bay. The Brewers are run by Rays alum Matt Arnold, and that man does love a three-team trade. They can find great production on the margins, as they have this season with Jake Bauers. And they are unafraid to deal star players as their contracts expire, as they did in recent years with Corbin Burnes, Devin Williams and Freddy Peralta. Where Milwaukee really excels is scouting Latin America. It signed Chourio and outfielder Luis Lara out of Venezuela. They signed Made and Peña out of the Dominican.
These are the things that small-market teams would like to emulate. Do well in the draft. Don’t stay static on the margins of the roster. And excel in finding stars out of the international market. If it was easy, every team would do it.
Do you think we have seen the last of Shohei Ohtani as a pitcher/starter? — Tae K.
I do not. He will pitch again. But how the Dodgers deploy him will be fascinating.
Multiple things can be true:
1. Shohei Ohtani might be the best pitcher in the world.
He demonstrated that during his 14 starts this season. He posted a 1.79 ERA while striking out 10 batters per nine innings. And he did that while toting the responsibility of batting leadoff as the designated hitter most days in between outings. He looked, in a word, awesome.
2. As he enters his mid-30s, Ohtani probably cannot complete a full season as a two-way player.
The basic story of Ohtani’s professional life is people within baseball telling him, “Hey! You can’t do that,” and Ohtani responding, “Well, actually, I can.” But Father Time is undefeated, and Ohtani has learned that the two-way load is far tougher to shoulder at 32 than it was at 27. He is currently on the injured list dealing with problems with his neck, knee and biceps. And there may be other maladies the famously private Ohtani has not revealed. Suffice to say, he is quite banged up, and no one within the Dodgers organization is thrilled about the situation.
Advertisement
These two facts — Ohtani’s greatness and his fallibility — present the Dodgers with a conflict. There is a clear compromise: the team should ask him to spend the first half of the season as a hitter and then use the second half to build up arm strength so he can be available to pitch in October. Problem solved!
Well, not exactly. Ohtani has agency in this situation. He may not want to give up the full-season two-way dream so easily. He may still want to prove that he can do in his 30s what he did in his 20s. He may still want to say, “Well, actually, I can.” And the Dodgers may not want to scuffle with the face of the franchise. It will be a delicate dance.
How Ohtani feels about his future is unclear. He has not spoken to reporters since Sept. 7, and did not accompany the club on its current trip to Miami and Cincinnati. But he has been staunch his entire career about wanting to remain a two-way player. “The reason why I’m a two-way player is because that’s who I am,” he said during the 2025 postseason. “And it’s what I can do.”
I still think he can be a two-way player, and I would be shocked if he tried to only hit moving forward. But the prospect of him being a healthy two-way player over the course of a 162-game season feels more like a fantasy than a reality. Then again, Ohtani has shown us, over and over in his career, that he can make dreams come true.
Catchers were the overwhelming best at ABS challenges, but I am curious how they fared at challenging as batters compared to batters at other positions. — Anonymous
Interesting premise.
I looked this up and found essentially no correlation. Now, there may be a connection, because while I am not a math wizard, I don’t think one unfinished season provides enough data for a sufficient sample size. At least this year, there is little evidence that, as hitters, catchers perform better than other hitters with ABS.
Dillon Dingler entered Monday’s games rated as the best challenger among catchers, according to FanGraphs. But as a hitter? Dingler graded below average. Same story for Hunter Goodman and J.T. Realmuto, the two catchers rated best behind Dingler.
Among the hitters, there were two catchers rated in Savant’s top 10 for ABS efficiency: Tyler Stephenson and Gabriel Moreno. Iván Herrera came in at No. 14. But then no catcher appears on the leaderboard until Brandon Valenzuela at No. 34. So, like I said, interesting premise, but no real correlation that this knucklehead who flunked geometry in high school can find.
Advertisement
For the last couple of decades, Major League Baseball has seemed to have a major “household name” gap with the NBA and NFL, and Rob Manfred once addressed this by complaining that Mike Trout wasn’t doing more to make himself famous. How is the league working to grow its fanbase and promote its product? — Alex R.
The owners are planning to lock out the players when the collective bargaining agreement expires on Dec. 1.
What are your most realistic thoughts on the lockout? — pollrobb
When I talk to people in baseball about the lockout, they usually say some version of the same thing: they really don’t know what will happen, but they think it will be bad. The negotiations will be contentious. The rhetoric will be vicious. They may well miss games.
My guess — and I will repeat that this is a guess — is that the lockout resolves at some point in March, with enough time to cram a 162-game season into the calendar, in a result similar to the last lockout. I do not foresee the players caving and accepting a salary cap. But it is also hard to identify, in that scenario, what would trigger the owners to stop pushing for one. Genuinely, I do not know how it will go, and anyone who tells you they do is probably overselling their insight.
Why would the players and league not work on solving 100 small things in negotiation now and figure out the big topic at the end? Is it really going to wreck what they have while fighting over billions of dollars? I truly enjoy the game and can’t believe they say it can all wait until December, so they can blame each other. Why not now? — Lynn Z.
To be fair, the two sides have traded a variety of proposals on issues besides the salary cap. They are negotiating. But the small stuff is small for a reason. And the big thing — the potential implementation of a salary cap — is much bigger than anything on the table in the previous round of negotiations. For the owners, the possibility of a cap means billions of dollars gained in franchise values. But for the players, accepting a cap means the collapse of the free-market system that the union has fought so strenuously to maintain for decades. These are existential questions for both sides. And neither side will be inclined to budge until the calendar flips into 2027 and spring training draws closer. So, buckle up. It is going to be a long, bumpy ride.

item.content:encoded:
CINCINNATI — Josue De Paula is in his element in the batter’s box. He carries himself like a guy who knows his importance to the Los Angeles Dodgers depends on how well he can command himself within those 24 square feet of chalk lines. De Paula asserts himself with a confident shake of the head after each pitch outside the strike zone.
Advertisement
Some head shakes are more exaggerated than others. Each demonstrates the same message: De Paula is not going to give in.
“I just want to feel saucy when I’m up there, you know what I’m saying?” De Paula told The Athletic this week. “I feel like I’m in control, not you. … I want my pitch. Come in the zone. Let’s go.”
This is who De Paula wants to be. He describes hitting as “aggressive patience,” an approach that puts him on the attack.
“It’s almost like a war for me in my head,” De Paula said. “I look confident. I look saucy. I feel saucy when I’m in the box, so it’s like, ‘Hey bro, let’s keep it rocking.’”
It took four games for De Paula to inspire fascination within the Dodgers dynasty, where his every at-bat feels like a must-watch example of how to command a zone. Of the first 37 big-league pitches De Paula saw outside of the strike zone, he swung at just five. He made it 17 plate appearances without striking out before going down swinging in the seventh inning and looking in the ninth in the Dodgers’ 4-0 win over the Reds on Tuesday. De Paula does not seem fazed that he is just 2 for 14 (.143) since being called up, including five hitless at-bats in his first game in the leadoff spot.
That’s because he believes in his process. A day earlier, De Paula battled back from down in the count against Reds lefty Nick Lodolo, a former All-Star. The left-handed batter took a 2-2 fastball just below the knees, crouched and shook his head. A pitch later, De Paula walked for the fifth time in his short career.
The clip of the head shake drew a chuckle from the proprietor of the “Soto Shuffle” himself, Juan Soto, who, like De Paula, once honed his craft at the El Niche Baseball Academy in the Dominican city of Santo Domingo.
Josue De Paula live reaction to you trying to get him to chase. https://t.co/CrmRSnDVgO pic.twitter.com/dbXGz8WYL0
— Chad Moriyama (@ChadMoriyama) September 14, 2026
“El loco mío,” Soto shared to his Instagram story in Spanish, stamping his approval with a laughing emoji. My guy.
Advertisement
“I swear I wasn’t trying to do like the whole thing,” De Paula said with a laugh. “I just got into my legs, and I was shaking my head … but I’m not mad. That’s not a bad player to look like.”
De Paula, 21, feels like an injection of youthful exuberance for baseball’s oldest lineup. The Brooklyn-born son of a Dominican father (and relative of NBA veterans Stephon Marbury and Sebastian Telfair) speaks with a thick New York accent and oozes the confidence of a player who carries that swagger into the box.
De Paula is the crown jewel of a Dodgers farm system that is expected to prolong this run of excellence. Last week, he became the first position player ever to be called up directly from Double A by this Andrew Friedman-led front office group.
De Paula is here because he can hit, has always hit, and the Dodgers need him to hit. De Paula is here to serve as the Dodgers’ designated hitter, at least until Shohei Ohtani returns from the injured list. No one with the Dodgers, however, is ruling out the possibility that De Paula could help them in October as they seek a third consecutive World Series title.
“I hope he makes our decision hard,” manager Dave Roberts said.
Through De Paula’s torrid run through the Dodgers’ farm system, officials raved about his keen ability to pick up the baseball, make proper swing decisions and recognize spin.
“He doesn’t give away any pitches, which I love, let alone give away any at-bats,” Roberts said.
Pair that with a preternatural ability to make contact, and De Paula entered this season as one of the highly-regarded young hitters in the league. The Dodgers implemented a change to De Paula’s swing this year, lowering his hands and opening up his resulting bat path to keep the barrel in the zone longer. That has allowed him to access more power by pulling more fly balls and has made him a lethal producer at Double A.
Advertisement
De Paula slugged 27 home runs this season in Double A, more than double what he had in any of his first four professional seasons. His first hit Sunday in Miami was a mammoth upper-deck shot to right field on the kind of awe-inspiring swing that has come much more easily for De Paula than in years past.
“When all those things are kind of clicking, it’s tough for any pitcher to compete with,” hitting coach Robert Van Scoyoc said. “So it’s been very impressive so far.”
De Paula became a Dodger partially as a byproduct of the COVID-19 pandemic, which shut down the New York baseball season and prompted De Paula’s father, Josue Sr., to send him to the Dominican Republic to work at El Niche under Cristian “Niche” Batista.
“It was like stepping into a whole other world,” De Paula said.
It was there, during an offseason workout, that De Paula met Soto, who broke into the big leagues at 19 years old with the kind of swaggering command of the batter’s box that De Paula hopes to replicate. Rather than enter the amateur draft, De Paula signed directly with the Dodgers as an international amateur for a bonus of just under $400,000. De Paula estimated that, in one of his two tryouts with the organization and with several of the club’s brass in attendance, he collected nine hits in 10 at-bats.
“I killed,” De Paula said, reliving the memory as if it just happened.
He has hit ever since, ascending to the top of prospect lists. His list of star-studded admirers grew, too. After accompanying Soto in being represented by super agent Scott Boras, De Paula was asked by Boras to name some of his favorite players. De Paula selected Elly De La Cruz, who at that time was set for his first season as a breakout star for the Cincinnati Reds but was already dominating the minor leagues. Boras invited De Paula to his Newport Beach offices in Southern California after that and surprised him by bringing De La Cruz.
Advertisement
The two have remained close, working out together in the Miami area in the winters. Friday, just before he made his major-league debut against the Marlins in Miami, De Paula called De La Cruz on FaceTime. When they met up again this week in Cincinnati, they posed for a picture.
“I’m really happy for what he’s doing,” De La Cruz said.
De Paula sees a kinship between De La Cruz and Soto.
“We’re all killers,” De Paula said with a knowing smirk.
When De Paula spent his first spring training in big-league camp with the Dodgers in 2025, he quickly heard from Mookie Betts. The former Gold Glove right fielder wanted to make De Paula and fellow newcomers Zyhir Hope and Justin Dean feel welcome, so over dinner at a Phoenix-area soul food restaurant, he talked shop. When De Paula went out for early defensive work in the outfield this week, he had Roberts and Betts at different points offer some advice.
Now in a clubhouse filled with stars, De Paula said he feels at home. Whether he stays there heading into October will depend on how the rest of the regular season goes. The first few games have left a strong first impression.
“It’s a slow heartbeat,” Van Scoyoc said. “He’s not overwhelmed at all. It seemed like he picked up where he left off in Double A. … I wouldn’t say it’s surprising, but it’s just nice to see.”
Ohtani is expected to return from his nagging biceps and knee injuries by year’s end. De Paula has a lack of defensive utility at this point. While he did play in left field on Sunday, the Dodgers still want to work on getting De Paula to “value” the defensive side of the ball first, Roberts said. That means his path to the Dodgers’ postseason roster will likely be as a left-handed bat off the bench, essentially the role the club envisioned for Dalton Rushing before his most recent IL stint.
Advertisement
That decision is still up in the air, Roberts said. There will be “growing pains,” as Roberts said after Tuesday’s performance. The manager said he “didn’t love” the quality of De Paula’s at-bats. But October is a scenario De Paula feels he will be ready for.
“Especially in big moments, I feel like my mind just goes to a whole ‘nother level,” De Paula said. “Especially competing. The bigger the moment is … it’s like the more my mind hyper-focuses. So when I’m hyper-focused like that a lot, it’s dangerous.”
